lines.text: take the action $\pi$ gives for $S$; see $R$ and $S'$

verification.note: Pseudocode compared with the page image; the implementation is checked against the draft's examples by the lab checks.

explainer.problem: Estimate $v_\pi$ from experience, like Monte Carlo, but update after every step, using the current estimate of the next state: learning a guess from a guess.

derivation.tex: v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid S_t = s] = \mathbb{E}_\pi[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t = s]
derivation.why: (6.3) is MC's target; (6.4) is the one DP and TD use.
Sample the expectation with one transition and use the current $V$ for $v_\pi$: (6.2).

example.text: Random walk with $V = 0.5$ everywhere and α = 0.1. The step from E to the right end (reward 1) gives target $1 + 0 = 1$, TD error 0.5 and $V(E) = 0.55$. Then the step from D to E gives target $0 + 0.55$, so $V(D) = 0.505$: the value propagates back one state at a time.

advantages: Learns during an episode, and also in continuing tasks.
Converges to $v_\pi$ for a fixed policy (in the mean for small α, with probability 1 for decreasing α).
Usually faster than constant-α MC on stochastic tasks (Figure 6.7).
limitations: Its target is biased by the current estimates.
Which of TD and MC learns faster in general is not settled (p. 148).

comparisons.point: Monte Carlo waits for the full return $G_t$ instead of bootstrapping from $V(S_{t+1})$.
DP backs up the full expectation using a model; TD backs up one sample.

name: Sarsa

lines.text: Start with any $Q(s, a)$; $Q$ of a terminal state is 0
set $S$; choose $A$ from $S$ ε-greedily with respect to $Q$
choose $A'$ from $S'$ ε-greedily with respect to $Q$
$Q(S, A) \leftarrow Q(S, A) + \alpha[R + \gamma Q(S', A') - Q(S, A)]$

output: $Q$ for the ε-greedy policy being followed

verification.note: Pseudocode compared with the page image; the implementation is checked against the draft's examples by the lab checks.

explainer.problem: Learn to act well (control) from experience, step by step, by learning the action values of the ε-greedy policy actually being followed and making it greedier over time.

example.text: One transition with $Q(S_t, A_t) = -2$, $R_{t+1} = -1$, $Q(S_{t+1}, \cdot) = (-1, -3)$, γ = 1 and α = 0.5. If the ε-greedy next action is the worse one, Sarsa's target is $-1 + (-3) = -4$, its TD error is −2, and $Q(S_t, A_t)$ becomes −3.

advantages: Accounts for its own exploration, so it learns the safer path on cliff walking and earns more online (Figure 6.13).
Learns during episodes, so it copes with tasks where some policies never terminate (windy gridworld, p. 157).
limitations: Learns the value of the exploring policy, not of the optimal one, unless ε is reduced over time.
Its convergence result needs ε to decrease, e.g. ε = 1/t (p. 155).

comparisons.point: Q-learning bootstraps from $\max_a Q(S_{t+1}, a)$ instead of the action actually taken next.
Monte Carlo ES learns Q from whole-episode returns with exploring starts.

lines.text: Start with any $Q(s, a)$; $Q$ of a terminal state is 0
choose $A$ from $S$ ε-greedily with respect to $Q$; take it; see $R$ and $S'$
$Q(S, A) \leftarrow Q(S, A) + \alpha[R + \gamma \max_a Q(S', a) - Q(S, A)]$

verification.note: Pseudocode compared with the page image; the implementation is checked against the draft's examples by the lab checks.

explainer.problem: Learn the optimal action-value function $q_*$ directly from experience, whatever (sufficiently exploring) policy is generating it.

example.text: The same transition as for Sarsa: $Q(S_t, A_t) = -2$, $R_{t+1} = -1$, $Q(S_{t+1}, \cdot) = (-1, -3)$. Q-learning's target is $-1 + \max(-1, -3) = -2$, its TD error is 0, and $Q(S_t, A_t)$ stays −2, even if the next action actually taken is the worse one.

advantages: Simple to analyse, with convergence proofs (p. 157).
limitations: Its online performance can be worse than Sarsa's: on cliff walking it learns the edge path and keeps falling while exploring (Figure 6.13).
All state–action pairs must keep being updated.

comparisons.point: Sarsa's target uses the next action actually chosen, so it evaluates the exploring policy.
Value iteration applies the same max backup with a full model.
